input: The Nusselt number is a dimensionless quantity that is widely used in the study of heat transfer, and it can be understood as the ratio of convective to conductive heat transfer at a surface. What this means, in practical terms, is that the number provides a way of comparing how effectively heat is carried away from a surface by the movement of a fluid with how effectively that same heat would be transferred by conduction through a stationary layer of fluid resting against the surface. When the Nusselt number has a value near 1, it tells us that convection and conduction are contributing at roughly comparable levels, so the moving fluid is not enhancing the transfer very much beyond what conduction alone would be able to achieve. When, on the other hand, the Nusselt number takes a large value, it indicates that convection is the dominant mechanism, and that the movement of the fluid is responsible for the great majority of the heat transferred at the surface, with conduction through the near-surface layer playing a comparatively minor role. It is worth keeping in mind that the number, being a ratio, is concerned with the relative importance of the two mechanisms, and it does not by itself say anything about how large either rate of transfer actually is in absolute terms, which is a point that is often overlooked by students who are meeting the quantity for the first time.
target: The Nusselt number is the ratio of convective to conductive heat transfer at a surface. Convection is transfer by a moving fluid; conduction is transfer through a stationary layer. The Nusselt number compares the two rates for the same surface. A value near 1 means the two rates are comparable: the moving fluid transfers heat at about the rate conduction alone would give, and fluid motion adds little to the transfer at the surface. A large value means convection dominates: the moving fluid carries most of the heat transferred at the surface, and conduction through the near-surface layer accounts for a small part of the total. The number is a ratio, and a ratio states a balance, not a magnitude. A surface can show a large Nusselt number while the absolute rate of transfer at that surface is low, because the conductive rate it is compared against is lower still. A surface can equally show a modest value while the absolute rate is high, because both mechanisms are then contributing strongly and the comparison between them stays close. The teaching point of the number is the identification of the governing mechanism. Where convection dominates, an account of the transfer stands or falls on its description of the fluid motion. Where the two mechanisms are comparable, the conduction description of the layer next to the surface carries the same weight, and neglecting it misstates the transfer even if the convection description is exact. The number also disciplines comparison between cases: two surfaces are compared through it only when the comparison is restated as a comparison of balances, never as a comparison of rates.
